name: Detox teas / juice cleanses
lead: Detox teas and juice cleanses are consumer products and short-term diets marketed as ways to remove unspecified 'toxins' from the body. People use them hoping for a leaner, less bloated look, clearer skin and a fresh start to a diet or fitness push. They belong to the wider category of detoxification, which also includes fasting, colon cleansing and restricted diets.[1][3]

Proponents say modern food and the environment leave contaminants that accumulate in the body and that a cleanse helps release them.[1][2] The British Dietetic Association lists the usual promises as rapid weight loss, better digestion, improved skin, hair and nails, more energy, stronger immunity and reduced cellulite.[3]

Reviews report limited support for the claims. A 2026 mini-review of diet and detox teas for weight loss found ten studies and limited support for weight-loss benefit, with some serious adverse health outcomes in case reports,[4] and a 2015 critical review in the Journal of Human Nutrition and Dietetics called for independent regulatory review of detox products.[1]

paras: Detoxification in the alternative-medicine sense aims to remove unspecified toxins said to build up in the body. Common forms include dieting, fasting, eating only certain foods, colon cleansing, chelation and some intravenous therapies [1]. Detox diets may limit intake to water or juice, remove fats or highly processed foods, or emphasise fibre [1].
Detox teas are herbal blends sold with similar promises. The reference material used for this article does not describe their ingredients or regulation in detail.

By the 19th century the theory of autointoxication, in which constipation was thought to produce toxins that are reabsorbed, had gained support, and it fell out of favour in the early 20th century. Walter Alvarez's 1919 JAMA article on so-called autointoxication symptoms is often cited as a turning point [1].

Interest returned with the growth of alternative medicine in the 1970s [1]. Juice-based cleansing drew on figures such as Norman Walker, who built an early juicer in 1936, and Jay Kordich in the 1990s [2].

The British Dietetic Association says detox teas usually work as laxatives, which carries some risk.[3] The 2026 mini-review says a small number of experimental studies suggested modest effects on body weight or metabolic outcomes, while most of the evidence was case reports and product analyses, some describing serious adverse outcomes.[4]

A 2021 case report in Cureus described a previously healthy 51-year-old woman who developed acute severe hyponatremia, with increased urination, after regular use of an over-the-counter detox tea; she recovered after intensive care, and the authors identified similar cases in the literature.[5]

Prolonged fasting recommended by some detox regimens can be dangerous, whereas a single short fast is considered unlikely to cause harm.[1] A 2018 report in the American Journal of Kidney Diseases linked a green-smoothie cleanse to acute oxalate nephropathy.[1] The tea-related hyponatremia case and the mini-review's adverse-event reports are described above.[4][5]
Commentators also note that belief in detox can delay effective treatment of disease, and describe individual cases of serious harm reported in news media.[1]

No trials of detox teas or juice cleanses for appearance outcomes such as skin were found. The 2026 mini-review of ten studies on diet and detox teas for weight loss found limited support for weight-loss benefit,[4] and reviews of detox diets more broadly are summarised above.[1]
No studies found on detox teas specifically for appearance outcomes. Reviews of detox diets more broadly are summarised above [1].

card.summary: Teas and cleanses sold to flush out 'toxins'; reviews find no good evidence they do.
card.note: Prolonged fasting and some cleanses have documented harms.

quick.overview:
Detox teas and juice cleanses are marketed as ways to purge toxins, with promised benefits such as clearer skin and a leaner look.

Published reviews have found no compelling evidence that detox diets remove toxins or help with weight beyond short-term loss that is regained.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say cleansing helps the body release accumulated contaminants. Clinicians note that the liver and kidneys already process most ingested toxins.
quick.risks: Prolonged fasting can be dangerous, and a kidney injury case was linked to a green-smoothie cleanse. Belief in detox can also delay medical care.

chain: Tea or juice-only plan replaces usual eating for a period
Short-term loss of water weight and reduced bloating
Leaner-looking midsection; skin and energy benefits are claimed
angle.text: Users run a tea or juice cleanse for a few days to look leaner and less bloated, and some link it to clearer skin. The BDA says quick weight change on such plans mostly reflects water and glycogen and often returns when normal eating resumes.
